case_name: Barendra Kumar Ghosh v. Emperor (Post Office Murder Case)

pages.text:
IN THE PRIVY COUNCIL
APPEAL FROM THE HIGH COURT OF JUDICATURE AT FORT WILLIAM IN BENGAL
Barendra Kumar Ghosh ... Appellant
versus
Emperor ... Respondent
Coram: Lord Sumner, Sir John Edge, Lord Carson
Judgment Dated: 23 January 1925

LORD SUMNER:
1. The appellant was convicted of murder under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, in connection with the armed robbery and murder of the sub-postmaster at the Sankaritolla Post Office in Calcutta on 3 August 1923.

2. Facts: Three men entered the post office demanding money while the appellant stood outside on the verandah holding a firearm. Shots were fired inside the room causing the immediate death of the sub-postmaster. The appellant fled when pursued and was apprehended with a loaded pistol in his hand. The appellant argued that he did not fire the fatal shot and only stood outside as a guard under duress.

3. Decision & Legal Principle: Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code lays down the principle of joint liability in common intention. Section 34 deals with the doing of separate acts, similar or diverse, by several persons; if all are done in furtherance of a common intention, each person is liable for the result of them all as if he had done them himself. As famously observed: 'They also serve who only stand and wait.' Standing guard to assist perpetrators or prevent interception constitutes active participation in furtherance of common intention. Conviction under Section 302 read with Section 34 affirmed.
